newsitem.title: USA: Jewish groups praise Swiss Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Jewish groups praise Swiss Holocaust fund.

text.p: Jewish leaders Wednesday hailed a decision by Switzerland's biggest banks to create a Holocaust memorial fund, but the New York City Council said it still planned to hold hearings on whether it should bar Swiss banks from receiving deposits of city funds.
World Jewish Congress President Edgar Bronfman, who led the fight to get Switzerland to establish the fund, said, "We look forward to this development as marking a new chapter in our relationship."

A WJC spokesman said the organization had informed New York City Council President Peter Vallone that the Swiss had acted to set up a Holocaust memorial fund as called for in proposed council legislation that threatens to pull city funds from Swiss banks if it did not.
But a spokesman for Vallone said that hearings on the bill would go ahead as planned for Monday. He said the banks' decision to set up the fund a positive development.
The City Council said two weeks ago that it would consider withholding depositing funds into Swiss banks operating in New York unless a fund was set up by the Swiss government and the banks.

Switzerland's three largest banks announced that they would contribute $70 million to get the fund started. Bronfman said that the Swiss government gave him assurances Thursday that this was an "initial infusion" of money into the fund and did not prejudice a final settlement or contributions from the government.

The banks, Union Bank of Switzerland, Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp SBC, set up the fund after months of criticism from Jewish groups and leading U.S. politicians combined with an avalanche of embarrassing documents from the U.S. National Archives on how Swiss banks aided Germany during the Second World War.

Jewish groups have accused banks of hoarding the unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims and of stonewalling family members seeking to get back money that Jews stashed in neutral Switzerland to hide it from the Nazis.
Bankers said the contribution, already on deposit at the Swiss National Bank, underscored banks' willingness to come to grips with a problem that tarnished their image.
